suggestions.reason: The response is a written plan (a 'what I would do' narrative), not an actual execution with real tool calls and real file writes. All five assertions pass against this plan, but a skill that produces a plausible-sounding plan without actually running correctly would also pass all five. Consider adding an assertion that verifies the files are *actually written to disk* (e.g., 'The 12 core files exist under design-system/ in the project after the skill runs'), so grading can distinguish a genuine execution from a persuasive description of one.

suggestions.assertion: Mentions handling the case where a design-system/ folder already exists containing code files (does not blindly overwrite)
suggestions.reason: The assertion only checks that the case is *mentioned* — a single sentence would satisfy it. A stronger assertion would verify that the skill *actually stops or reroutes* when it detects code files (e.g., checks that no Write call was made to a directory that already contained .tsx files). As written, any response that says 'I would ask first' passes, even if the implementation blindly overwrites.

suggestions.assertion: Names all 12 core templates to be created
suggestions.reason: The assertion is satisfied if all 12 names appear anywhere in the output. It would not catch a response that names all 12 but groups them differently or omits a file during actual execution. If execution is real, pairing this assertion with a file-system check would make it discriminating.

eval_feedback.overall: All five assertions pass cleanly and the evidence is unambiguous within the plan. The main gap is that the output is a hypothetical plan rather than a live run — the evals are well-designed for checking the plan's content, but they cannot distinguish a good plan from correct execution. Adding at least one assertion that checks a concrete artefact (e.g., a file on disk or a real tool call log) would make the eval suite more robust.
